newsitem.title: USA: Man injured, two held hostage in Texas standoff.
newsitem.headline: Man injured, two held hostage in Texas standoff.

text.p: One man was wounded and two people were taken hostage on Sunday in a standoff between police and a separatist group in west Texas, officials said.

Laureen Chernow, a spokeswoman with the Department of Public Safety, said one man suffered a gunshot wound to the shoulder and two people were seized as hostages near a compound belonging to the self-styled Republic of Texas, which believes the state was annexed illegally in 1845 and that it should be an independent nation.

Chernow said FBI agents were joining local and state police units outside the remote compound where Republic of Texas members, led by self-styled ambassador Richard McLaren, have been holed up since December.

Group members confirmed they had two hostages but blamed police for the violence. They also denied the injured man was shot in the shoulder, saying he was only hit by flying glass in an exchange of gunfire and had been released for medical treatment.
"We have two prisoners that we have captured: they are both spies for the foreign government," a man identifying himself as "White Eagle" told Reuters by telephone from inside the compound.
He said local police had arrested the Republic's chief of security, Bob Scheidt, early on Sunday and that the Republic took two civilians -- a husband and wife -- hostage in retaliation.
The husband, identified as Joe Rowe, was injured when shots were fired and Republic leaders said they took another man hostage when they released Rowe for treatment.
White Eagle said the Republic would release the two hostages in exchange for the release of Scheidt and another Republic member who was recently arrested on contempt of court charges.

"We are not looking for anyone to die but if they have decided they want a war, they are going to get a war," he said, adding the Republic had sealed its compound and ordered allied militia members to capture federal agents across Texas.
"People are going to come out of the woodwork and take Texas back, they'll take the United States back too," he said.
McLaren has said his group's "defense forces" have thousands of members, but police dispute those claims. It is not clear how many Republic members are holed up inside the compound with McLaren.
The Republic of Texas emerged in 1995, demanding the resignation of Gov. George W. Bush and other state leaders as well as the removal of federal agencies from Texas.

State officials accuse the group of filing thousands of bogus liens against government agencies and private property owners, tying up the courts with what state Attorney General Dan Morales has called "paper terrorism".
McLaren was charged with contempt of court last December for failing to appear in a federal court in nearby Pecos on charges related to the liens.
